A man in his 20s with complex congenital heart disease that included D-transposition of the great arteries, single ventricle physiology (upstairs-downstairs configuration of the ventricles with a large ventricular septal defect with outflow extension), and Fontan circulation was admitted with lightheadedness and syncope that occurred while walking. He had previously been prescribed diltiazem 120 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily after an initial episode. He returned a few days later with persistent tachycardia and palpitations.

Heart rate of 183 beats per minute (bpm) in the emergency department.

- Electrocardiogram (ECG):  Image Title: Figure 1A and 1B - Electrocardiograms of a Narrow Complex Tachycardia  Image Description: Shows irregularly irregular tachycardia with grouped beating and intermittently visible P waves in lead V1. Rhythm strip shows 3 consistent beats grouped together with 560-millisecond duration.- Transesophageal echocardiogram:  Finding: No intracardiac thrombus detected.- Additional ECG after diltiazem:  Image Title: Figure 2A - ECG after diltiazem administration  Image Description: Regular narrow complex tachycardia with visible P waves in lead II, cycle length between visible P waves is 440 milliseconds.- ECG with adenosine:  Image Title: Figure 2B - ECG after adenosine administration  Image Description: Shows temporary heart block with continuation of supraventricular tachycardia with cycle length of 220 ms.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) with variable atrioventricular block

clinical_record:
A 39-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent fever, night sweats, a 15-kg weight loss, decreased appetite, dry cough, and shortness of breath. He had no significant medical history, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts, but lived in close quarters with 13 other inmates. On examination, his heart rate was elevated, blood pressure was low but responsive to fluids, and he had fine tremors. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP), and raised inflammatory markers. Anteroposterior chest radiography revealed numerous bilateral tiny nodules throughout both lung fields. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed innumerable widespread pulmonary nodules, a few cavitary lesions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Because of his headache, an MRI of the brain was obtained, which demonstrated vasogenic edema in the left posterior insula and temporoparietal cortex, intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the same region, and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement—findings consistent with hemorrhagic meningoencephalitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

clinical_record:
A white woman in her 20s with unremarkable medical and ocular history presented with decreased vision in her right eye. Symptoms began 4 days prior to presentation, when she was struck by lightning directly to the right forehead while hiking.

- Uncorrected visual acuity measured 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS- Pupils were symmetric, with no relative afferent pupillary defect- Initial anterior segment examination was normal with absence of cataract- Initial dilated fundus examination showed no apparent abnormalities in either eye- At 2 weeks: central macular thickening in fundus examination- At 7 weeks: mild posterior subcapsular cataract visible in right eye

Spectral-domain OCT findings:- Initial examination (4 days post-injury):   Image Description: Preserved foveal contour in both eyes without cystoid abnormalities. Right eye showed subtle irregularity of the outer retinal layers, most notable nasal to the fovea  - Two weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Intraretinal cystoid changes and subfoveal ellipsoid zone disruption in the right eye  - Seven weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Restoration of foveal contour with decreased cystoid abnormalities, small subfoveal hyporeflective space, and further loss of outer retinal layers in the nasal macula  - Four months post-injury:  Image Description: Persistent subfoveal hyporeflective space in the inner retina with interval restoration of subfoveal outer retinal structures

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Lightning-induced retinopathy with delayed-onset cystoid macular abnormalities

clinical_record:
A woman in her 80s presented to the emergency department with altered mental status, weakness, slurred speech, emesis, and headache. Emergency medical services found her pulse rate in the 20s. Her initial vital signs in the emergency department were blood pressure of 100/73 mm Hg, heart rate of 49 beats/min, respiratory rate of 27 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on a nonrebreather mask.

Patient required intubation for airway protection.

- Imaging Studies:    1. Computed tomography of the head: No acute pathology    2. Chest radiography: Showed pulmonary consolidation    3. Electrocardiogram (ECG):       Image Title: Electrocardiogram During Transcutaneous Pacing       Image Description: ECG showing intrinsic junctional rhythm at rate of about 60 beats/min, and TCP delivering stimuli at about 75 beats/min. Narrow QRS complexes without visible preceding P waves at rate of about 60 beats/min.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Septic shock with anuric kidney failure
